rules.name: Run key value launches from a user-writable directory
rules.description: A Run or RunOnce autostart value points into a temp, AppData, ProgramData or Public directory, a common location for dropped payloads that persist across logons.
rules.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys

rules.name: Run key value invokes a script interpreter or LOLBin
rules.description: A Run or RunOnce value launches powershell, mshta, wscript, cscript, rundll32 or regsvr32 directly, a common fileless persistence pattern.
rules.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys

rules.name: Image File Execution Options Debugger value set
rules.description: A Debugger value was written under Image File Execution Options, which makes Windows launch an attacker program in place of the named binary (accessibility-feature backdoors, hijacks).
rules.technique_name: Event Triggered Execution: Image File Execution Options Injection

rules.name: SilentProcessExit monitor process configured
rules.description: A MonitorProcess value under SilentProcessExit makes Windows launch a program when the target process exits, used for stealthy persistence and credential dumping from lsass.
rules.technique_name: Event Triggered Execution: Image File Execution Options Injection

rules.name: AppInit_DLLs configured
rules.description: AppInit_DLLs lists DLLs injected into every process that loads user32.dll; a non-empty value is a classic persistence and injection mechanism.
rules.technique_name: Event Triggered Execution: AppInit DLLs

rules.name: AppCertDlls key modified
rules.description: A value under Session Manager AppCertDlls was written; DLLs listed there are loaded into every process that calls CreateProcess-family APIs.
rules.technique_name: Event Triggered Execution: AppCert DLLs

rules.name: Service ImagePath points to a user-writable directory
rules.description: A service ImagePath was set to a temp, AppData, ProgramData, Public or Downloads path, typical of malware installing itself as a service.
rules.technique_name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service

rules.name: Service ImagePath runs a shell or script interpreter
rules.description: A service ImagePath contains cmd /c, powershell or similar, the pattern left by PsExec-like tooling and many post-exploitation frameworks installing one-shot services.
rules.technique_name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service

rules.name: Windows Defender exclusion added
rules.description: A value was created under a Windows Defender Exclusions key (paths, extensions or processes), commonly done by malware to hide its files from scanning.
rules.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

rules.name: Windows Defender protection disabled via registry
rules.description: Defender policy or real-time protection values (DisableAntiSpyware, DisableRealtimeMonitoring, DisableBehaviorMonitoring, DisableIOAVProtection) were set to 1.
rules.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

rules.name: UAC disabled or admin consent prompt removed
rules.description: EnableLUA was set to 0 or ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to 0 under Policies\System, turning off User Account Control elevation prompts.
rules.technique_name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Bypass User Account Control

rules.name: LSA protection (RunAsPPL) disabled
rules.description: RunAsPPL under the LSA key was set to 0, removing protected-process shielding for lsass and easing credential dumping.
rules.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

rules.name: LSA security or authentication package modified
rules.description: Security Packages, Authentication Packages or Notification Packages under the LSA key were written; malicious SSP/AP DLLs (for example mimilib) load into lsass this way.
rules.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Security Support Provider

attrs.value_data: kerberos msv1_0 schannel wdigest tspkg pku2u mimilib

rules.name: WDigest UseLogonCredential enabled
rules.description: UseLogonCredential=1 under WDigest makes Windows keep cleartext passwords in lsass memory, a prerequisite for credential dumping.
rules.technique_name: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory

rules.name: Remote Desktop enabled via registry
rules.description: fDenyTSConnections was set to 0 under Terminal Server, enabling inbound RDP on the host.
rules.technique_name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol

rules.name: RDP Network Level Authentication disabled
rules.description: UserAuthentication was set to 0 for the RDP-Tcp listener, removing NLA and exposing the login screen to pre-authentication attacks.
rules.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

rules.name: Winlogon Shell or Userinit changed from default
rules.description: The Winlogon Shell or Userinit value was set to something other than explorer.exe or userinit.exe, which runs an attacker program at every logon.
rules.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Winlogon Helper DLL

rules.name: COM object server registered in a user-writable location
rules.description: A per-user CLSID InprocServer32 or LocalServer32 was set to a temp, AppData or Public path; COM hijacking loads attacker code whenever the legitimate class is instantiated.
rules.technique_name: Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking

rules.name: PowerShell script block logging disabled
rules.description: EnableScriptBlockLogging was set to 0 in the PowerShell policy key, blinding the most useful PowerShell audit trail.
rules.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging

rules.name: DGA-like long random label
rules.description: The queried name has a 30+ character alphanumeric label that mixes letters and digits, typical of algorithmically generated domains and some tunnelling payloads.
rules.technique_name: Dynamic Resolution: Domain Generation Algorithms

rules.name: Very long TXT query name
rules.description: A TXT query name of 100+ characters is characteristic of DNS tunnelling and exfiltration tools that pack data into the question.
rules.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol

rules.name: NULL record query
rules.description: NULL-type DNS queries have no legitimate everyday use and are the signature transport of iodine-style IP-over-DNS tunnels.
rules.technique_name: Application Layer Protocol: DNS

rules.name: Near-maximum length DNS label
rules.description: A label of 55+ characters on a name with several more labels is how tunnelling tools maximise bytes per query.
rules.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol

rules.name: Hex-encoded data in a DNS label
rules.description: A label made of 32+ hexadecimal characters, often a hash or encoded file chunk, prefixes a multi-label name, a common DNS exfiltration encoding.
rules.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol

rules.name: Dynamic DNS provider domain queried
rules.description: The query is under a free dynamic-DNS provider (duckdns, no-ip, ddns.net, dyndns, hopto and similar) frequently used for attacker infrastructure that changes IP.
rules.technique_name: Dynamic Resolution

rules.name: Paste site queried (dead-drop resolver pattern)
rules.description: The query resolves a text paste service (pastebin, paste.ee, hastebin, rentry, ghostbin, ix.io, termbin), which malware uses to fetch C2 addresses or configuration.
rules.technique_name: Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver

rules.name: Anonymous file-drop service queried
rules.description: The query resolves an anonymous file-sharing or upload service (transfer.sh, anonfiles, file.io, 0x0.st, temp.sh, gofile, catbox), commonly used to exfiltrate staged data.
rules.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Web Service

rules.name: Tor onion gateway or .onion name queried
rules.description: The query is a .onion name or a clearnet Tor gateway (onion.ly, onion.to, tor2web and similar), a way to reach hidden services without running Tor.
rules.technique_name: Proxy: Multi-hop Proxy

rules.name: Root SSH login from a public address
rules.description: A successful ssh login as root came from a non-private source address, a direct administrative path that should rarely be reachable from the internet.
rules.technique_name: Valid Accounts

rules.name: Service account used sudo successfully
rules.description: A service or daemon account (www-data, nginx, postgres, nobody, svc-*, _name) ran sudo successfully; these accounts should not have interactive privilege escalation, which points to a compromised service.
rules.technique_name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Sudo and Sudo Caching

rules.name: Service account logged in over SSH
rules.description: A service or daemon account authenticated over ssh; such accounts normally have no login shell, so a success suggests a planted key or password.
rules.technique_name: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts

rules.name: Service account interactive console login
rules.description: A service or daemon account logged in at the console, which is never expected for non-human accounts.
rules.technique_name: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts

rules.name: RDP login from a public address
rules.description: A successful RDP logon came from a non-private source address, meaning RDP is exposed to the internet and a credential was accepted.
rules.technique_name: External Remote Services

rules.name: RDP login as a default account
rules.description: A successful RDP logon used the built-in Administrator, Guest or a default-named admin account, which should be renamed or disabled.
rules.technique_name: Valid Accounts: Default Accounts

rules.name: NTLM authentication accepted from a public address
rules.description: An NTLM logon succeeded from a non-private source; NTLM exposed to the internet enables relay, spraying and downgrade attacks.
rules.technique_name: Valid Accounts

rules.name: NTLM logon as Administrator (pass-the-hash indicator)
rules.description: A built-in Administrator account authenticated with NTLM rather than Kerberos, the typical signature of pass-the-hash lateral movement.
rules.technique_name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash

rules.name: Kerberos authentication as krbtgt
rules.description: The krbtgt account never logs on interactively; a Kerberos authentication attributed to it indicates a forged (golden) ticket.
rules.technique_name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket

rules.name: OAuth sign-in to a privileged account from a public address
rules.description: An OAuth sign-in succeeded for an admin-style account (admin, root, owner, global admin) from a non-private source, a high-value cloud identity use that merits review.
rules.technique_name: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts

rules.name: Unsigned module loaded from a temp directory
rules.description: An unsigned DLL or shared object was loaded from a temp directory, a staging location for sideloading and injected payloads.
rules.technique_name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading

rules.name: Unsigned module loaded from a user download, desktop or profile directory
rules.description: An unsigned DLL or shared object was loaded from a user-owned directory such as Downloads, Desktop, AppData, Public or a home cache, where users and droppers place side-loaded libraries.
rules.technique_name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading

rules.name: Module loaded from an injection-prone directory
rules.description: A module was loaded from a directory that is writable by users yet trusted by allow-lists (Windows\Tasks, Windows\Debug, PerfLogs, Recycle Bin, Users\Public), a typical drop spot for injected DLLs.
rules.technique_name: Process Injection: Dynamic-link Library Injection

rules.name: Shared object loaded from /tmp, /var/tmp or /dev/shm
rules.description: A shared object was loaded from a world-writable memory or temp directory, the staging location for LD_PRELOAD rootkits and in-memory implants.
rules.technique_name: Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking

rules.name: Unsigned kernel extension or driver loaded from a user directory
rules.description: An unsigned driver or kext was loaded from a temp, download, Public or home directory; kernel code staged from user-writable paths is a rootkit and BYOVD indicator.
rules.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Kernel Modules and Extensions

rules.name: Kernel extension loaded from outside the Extensions directories
rules.description: A kext was loaded from a path other than /System/Library/Extensions or /Library/Extensions, which is how unvetted kernel extensions are side-loaded.
rules.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Kernel Modules and Extensions

rules.name: Known vulnerable signed driver loaded (BYOVD)
rules.description: A driver commonly abused for kernel access by attackers (RTCore64, dbutil_2_3, gdrv, iqvw64e, capcom, winring0, asio and others) was loaded.
rules.technique_name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

rules.name: Credential-theft tool module loaded
rules.description: A module named like a well-known credential theft component (mimilib, mimidrv, memssp, wce) was loaded.
rules.technique_name: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory

rules.name: amsi.dll loaded from outside the system directories
rules.description: An amsi.dll was loaded from a path other than System32 or SysWOW64, the pattern of AMSI-bypass proxy DLLs placed next to a host executable.
rules.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
